teff.name: Teff
teff.summary: A cereal grass native to Ethiopia and Eritrea, cultivated for its edible seeds since at least 1000 BCE, and among the two countries' most important staple crops.

injera.name: Injera
injera.summary: A sour, spongy fermented flatbread traditionally made from teff flour, a staple central to dining in Ethiopian and Eritrean cuisine.

hararghe.name: Hararghe
hararghe.summary: Former province of eastern Ethiopia whose capital was the city of Harar.

berta-people.name: Berta people
berta-people.summary: Nilo-Saharan-speaking ethnic group living along the Sudan-Ethiopia border, also known as Benishangul or Funj, numbering roughly 200,000 in Ethiopia and 180,000 in Sudan.

gumuz-people.name: Gumuz
gumuz-people.summary: A Nilo-Saharan-speaking ethnic group of about 250,000 people in western Ethiopia and Sudan's Fazogli region.

koma-people.name: Koma people
koma-people.summary: A hill-dwelling ethnic group of the Atlantika Mountains, spread across dozens of villages on the Nigeria-Cameroon border.

kalokol-pillar-site.name: Namoratunga II
kalokol-pillar-site.summary: An archaeological pillar site on Lake Turkana in Kenya, whose name means 'people of stone,' dated to the Pastoral Neolithic with a radiocarbon sample around 2398 BC.

turkana-county.name: Turkana County
turkana-county.summary: Kenya's largest county by land area, in the northwest bordering Uganda, South Sudan, Ethiopia and Lake Turkana; home to the Turkana people, with a 2019 population of about 927,000.

kassala.name: Kassala
kassala.summary: The capital of Kassala state in eastern Sudan, on the Gash River, known for its fruit gardens and as a market and trade hub near the Eritrean border.

gash-group.name: Gash Group
gash-group.summary: A Neolithic culture that flourished from about 3000 to 1800 BCE in Eritrea and eastern Sudan, named for the Gash river.

kerma-culture.name: Kerma culture
kerma-culture.summary: An early civilization and kingdom in ancient Nubia, in what is now Sudan, flourishing from about 2500 to 1500 BCE and rivaling Egypt before Egypt's New Kingdom absorbed it.

land-of-punt.name: Land of Punt
land-of-punt.summary: An ancient kingdom known from Egyptian trade records for gold, resins, ebony, ivory and wild animals, likely located in the Horn of Africa; Egyptians called it 'Land of the God'.

twelfth-dynasty-of-egypt.name: Twelfth Dynasty
twelfth-dynasty-of-egypt.summary: A line of Egyptian pharaohs ruling from about 1991 to 1802 BCE, considered the peak of the Middle Kingdom, running from Amenemhat I to Sobekneferu.

tale-of-the-shipwrecked-sailor.name: Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor
tale-of-the-shipwrecked-sailor.summary: A Middle Kingdom Egyptian story about a sailor shipwrecked on an island who meets a giant snake before returning home.

hatshepsut.name: Hatshepsut
hatshepsut.summary: Sixth pharaoh of Egypt's Eighteenth Dynasty, ruling about 1479 to 1458 BC as only the second confirmed woman to rule Egypt in her own right, known for prosperity and major building projects.

deir-el-bahari.name: Deir el-Bahari
deir-el-bahari.summary: A complex of mortuary temples and tombs on the west bank of the Nile opposite Luxor, part of the Theban Necropolis, where reliefs depict Hatshepsut's expedition to Punt.

mentuhotep-iii.name: Mentuhotep III
mentuhotep-iii.summary: A pharaoh of Egypt's 11th Dynasty during the Middle Kingdom, remembered for his expedition to Punt and for architectural innovations.

wadi-hammamat.name: Wadi Hammamat
wadi-hammamat.summary: A valley in Egypt's Eastern Desert, exploited since pharaonic times for gold and stone quarries and used as a route between the Nile Valley and the Red Sea.

henenu-high-steward.name: Henenu
henenu-high-steward.summary: Egyptian noble and high steward to Mentuhotep III around 2000 BC, who reportedly reopened Egypt's trade routes to Punt and Libya.

mersa-gawasis.name: Mersa Gawasis
mersa-gawasis.summary: A small ancient Egyptian harbour on the Red Sea, used from the 12th Dynasty as a loading point for expeditions to Punt and the mines of Sinai.

agatharchides.name: Agatharchides
agatharchides.summary: A Greek historian and geographer from Cnidus, active in the 2nd century BC.

old-kingdom-of-egypt.name: Old Kingdom
old-kingdom-of-egypt.summary: An ancient Egyptian period lasting from about 2700 to 2200 BCE, called the Age of the Pyramids for the great pyramid-building kings of the Fourth Dynasty.

butana-group.name: Butana Group
butana-group.summary: A Neolithic culture in eastern Sudan flourishing from about 4000 to 2900 BC, known for decorated pottery, stone tools, and animal herding.

atbarah-river.name: Atbarah River
atbarah-river.summary: River in northeast Africa rising in Ethiopia and flowing about 805 km to join the Nile in Sudan, the last tributary the Nile receives before reaching the Mediterranean.

kingdom-of-kush.name: Kingdom of Kush
kingdom-of-kush.summary: An ancient kingdom in Nubia along the Nile in what is now Sudan and Egypt, rising from the city-state of Kerma and later ruling Egypt itself in the 8th century BCE under King Piye.

fourth-dynasty-of-egypt.name: Fourth Dynasty
fourth-dynasty-of-egypt.summary: A 'golden age' of ancient Egypt's Old Kingdom, lasting from about 2613 to 2498 BC and marked by peace, prosperity, and the height of pyramid building.

khufu.name: Khufu
khufu.summary: Second pharaoh of Egypt's Fourth Dynasty, reigning in the 26th century BC, credited with commissioning the Great Pyramid of Giza.

nehsi.name: Nehsi
nehsi.summary: An official of Nubian descent under pharaoh Hatshepsut, credited as chief treasurer with organising her trading expedition to Punt.

james-henry-breasted.name: James Henry Breasted
james-henry-breasted.summary: American archaeologist and Egyptologist (1865–1935), the first American to earn a doctorate in Egyptology, who founded the Oriental Institute at the University of Chicago in 1919.

afroasiatic-languages.name: Afroasiatic languages
afroasiatic-languages.summary: A family of about 400 languages spoken across West Asia, North Africa, and the Horn of Africa, with over 500 million native speakers; Arabic, Hausa, Oromo, Amharic, and Somali are its most-spoken members.

cushitic-languages.name: Cushitic languages
cushitic-languages.summary: Branch of the Afroasiatic language family spoken mainly in the Horn of Africa; major languages include Oromo, Somali, Beja, Afar, Hadiyya, Kambaata and Sidama.

omotic-languages.name: Omotic languages
omotic-languages.summary: A disputed grouping of languages spoken mainly in southwestern Ethiopia, with about 7.9 million speakers, generally classified within the Afroasiatic family.

nilo-saharan-languages.name: Nilo-Saharan languages
nilo-saharan-languages.summary: A proposed family of around 210 African languages spoken by roughly 70 million people mainly around the upper Nile and Chari rivers, named by linguist Joseph Greenberg in 1963.

dire-dawa.name: Dire Dawa
dire-dawa.summary: City in eastern Ethiopia, one of only two chartered cities in the country (with the capital Addis Ababa), and today an industrial centre with major markets.

agaw-people.name: Agaw
agaw-people.summary: A Cushitic ethnic group of Ethiopia's northern highlands and Eritrea, speaking the Agaw (Central Cushitic) languages; many historically practiced a 'Hebraic religion' and included Beta Israel Jews.

mekelle.name: Mekelle
mekelle.summary: Capital of Ethiopia's Tigray Region, about 780 km north of Addis Ababa, and the second-largest city in Ethiopia.
